questions.q: Where is the primary respiratory rhythm generator located in the brainstem, and which specific medullary sub-region acts as the central pacemaker for automatic breathing?
options: Pre-Bötzinger complex in the rostral ventrolateral medulla
Apneustic centre in the caudal pons
Pneumotaxic centre in the upper pons
Dorsal respiratory group in the dorsomedial medulla
questions.explain: The pre-Botzinger complex contains intrinsic pacemaker neurons (persistent Na+ current) that generate the basic inspiratory rhythm, driving the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups.

open.q: Name the specific anatomical region in the medulla oblongata that serves as the primary pacemaker for automatic respiratory rhythmogenesis.
accept: Pre-Botzinger complex (in the ventrolateral medulla / ventral respiratory group)

questions.q: How do the Dorsal Respiratory Group (DRG) and the Ventral Respiratory Group (VRG) in the medulla oblongata differ in their functional roles during quiet versus forced breathing?
options: DRG supports quiet inspiration and integrates visceral afferents; VRG is recruited mainly during forced breathing
DRG drives forced expiration; VRG generates quiet inspiration and integrates vagal afferents
DRG and VRG are pontine groups that switch inspiration on and off
DRG controls voluntary breathing; VRG controls breathing only during sleep
questions.explain: Quiet expiration is passive, so VRG expiratory neurons fire mainly when high minute ventilation demands active abdominal and internal intercostal contraction.

open.q: Contrast the roles of the medullary Dorsal Respiratory Group (DRG) and Ventral Respiratory Group (VRG) during quiet versus exercise breathing.
accept: DRG integrates sensory afferents (NTS) and drives quiet inspiration; VRG contains inspiratory and expiratory neurons recruited mainly during increased ventilatory demand and active forced expiration
DRG controls basic quiet inspiration; VRG is recruited for forceful inspiration and active expiration

questions.q: What is the physiological function of the inspiratory 'ramp' signal generated by medullary inspiratory neurons during quiet breathing?
options: Inspiratory firing rises gradually to produce smooth diaphragmatic contraction, then stops to allow passive expiration
Inspiratory neurons produce a brief maximal burst, followed by sustained contraction throughout expiration
The ramp signal inhibits phrenic motor neurons and prevents diaphragmatic contraction
The ramp maintains continuous diaphragmatic contraction without an expiratory pause
questions.explain: The ramp signal ensures smooth inflation of the lungs; the pneumotaxic center and pulmonary stretch receptors regulate the 'switch-off' point of the ramp, controlling inspiratory duration and respiratory rate.

open.q: Describe the temporal pattern and functional purpose of the medullary inspiratory 'ramp' signal.
accept: Firing gradually increases over ~2 seconds to produce smooth lung inflation and then abruptly stops for ~3 seconds to allow passive expiration
Gradual 2-second buildup for smooth inspiration followed by abrupt 3-second cessation for passive expiration

questions.q: How do the pontine 'pneumotaxic center' (nucleus parabrachialis / Kolliker-Fuse nucleus in the upper pons) and 'apneustic center' (lower pons) modulate medullary inspiratory activity?
options: The pneumotaxic centre limits inspiration; the apneustic centre promotes inspiratory activity
The pneumotaxic centre stops breathing for several minutes; the apneustic centre controls swallowing
The apneustic centre terminates inspiration; the pneumotaxic centre prolongs it
Both pontine centres generate the basic respiratory rhythm independently of the medulla
questions.explain: A strong pneumotaxic signal shortens inspiration (increasing rate to 30-40/min), whereas unopposed apneustic drive produces prolonged inspiratory gasps (apneusis).

open.q: Compare the effects of the pontine pneumotaxic center and apneustic center on the duration of inspiration and respiratory rate.
accept: Pneumotaxic center inhibits inspiration (shortens inspiratory duration, reduces tidal volume, increases respiratory rate); apneustic center prolongs inspiration (deep, sustained inspiratory drive)
Pneumotaxic limits inspiration and increases rate; apneustic prolongs inspiration

questions.q: What respiratory pattern ('apneusis' or apneustic breathing) results from a mid-pontine transection that disconnects the upper pontine pneumotaxic center while leaving the vagus nerves intact versus bilaterally transected?
options: Vagal stretch input can terminate inspiration; loss of both vagal and pontine off-switches may produce apneusis
Intact vagal input causes permanent apnea; vagotomy restores normal respiratory rhythm
Pontine transection causes Cheyne–Stokes breathing regardless of vagal input
Vagal and pontine pathways normally stimulate expiration, so their loss leaves breathing unchanged
questions.explain: Both the pontine pneumotaxic center and pulmonary vagal stretch afferents act as off-switches for the apneustic/inspiratory generator; losing both produces classic apneusis.

open.q: Which two neural inputs must both be interrupted to produce classic apneustic breathing (apneusis)?
accept: The upper pontine pneumotaxic center and bilateral vagus nerves (pulmonary stretch afferents)

questions.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors located, what is their direct proximate chemical stimulus, and why does acute arterial hypercapnia (elevated PaCO2) stimulate them far more rapidly than acute intravenous H+ (fixed metabolic acid)?
options: Ventral medulla; they respond to CSF H⁺ formed as CO₂ crosses the blood-brain barrier
Carotid body; they respond directly to arterial oxygen tension and haemoglobin saturation
Aortic arch; they respond to arterial hydrogen ions crossing directly into the medulla
Hypothalamus; they respond to plasma bicarbonate and sodium concentration
questions.explain: Because CSF has very low protein buffering capacity compared to blood, small increases in PaCO2 produce large drops in CSF pH, making PaCO2 (via CSF [H+]) the dominant minute-to-minute regulator of ventilation.

open.q: Explain why elevated arterial PCO2 stimulates central medullary chemoreceptors much more potently than an equivalent drop in arterial pH caused by fixed metabolic acids (e.g., lactic acid).
accept: CO2 readily crosses the blood-brain barrier and generates H+ in CSF (which has low buffering capacity) to stimulate central chemoreceptors, whereas H+ ions cross the blood-brain barrier poorly
CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier freely to form H+ in CSF, whereas H+ ions cannot easily cross the BBB

questions.q: Where are the peripheral chemoreceptors located, which cranial nerves carry their afferent signals to the medullary nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), and what are their chemical stimuli?
options: Carotid bodies (CN IX) and aortic bodies (CN X) respond to low PaO2, high PaCO2 and low pH
Carotid sinus and atrial appendage; innervated by CN VII and CN XII; stimulated only by glucose
Pulmonary veins; innervated by the phrenic nerve; stimulated by albumin
Renal juxtaglomerular apparatus; innervated by lumbar sympathetic nerves
questions.explain: Carotid bodies are the SOLE chemoreceptors in the human body that detect arterial hypoxemia (PaO2), and they also mediate the rapid hyperventilatory compensation for acute metabolic acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis). Key detail: Carotid bodies (Hering's nerve / CN IX) and aortic bodies (CN X); stimulated by low PaO2 (<60 mmHg), high PaCO2, and low pH.

open.q: Name the two peripheral chemoreceptor structures, their respective afferent cranial nerves, and the three arterial blood gas/acid-base changes that stimulate them.
accept: Carotid bodies (glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX) and aortic bodies (vagus nerve, CN X); stimulated by low PaO2, high PaCO2, and high [H+] (low pH)
Carotid bodies (CN IX) and aortic bodies (CN X); decreased PaO2, increased PaCO2, decreased pH

questions.q: What is the cellular transduction mechanism inside carotid body Type I (glomus) cells when arterial PaO2 falls below ~60 mmHg?
options: Hypoxia closes O₂-sensitive K⁺ channels, depolarizing glomus cells and triggering Ca²⁺-dependent transmitter release
Hypoxia opens K⁺ channels, hyperpolarizing glomus cells and suppressing transmitter release
Hypoxia activates insulin receptors on glomus cells and inhibits CN IX afferents
Glomus cells detect reduced haemoglobin saturation directly through surface integrins
questions.explain: Carotid bodies have the highest blood flow per gram of tissue in the body (~2,000 mL/100 g/min), so they sense dissolved arterial PaO2 rather than total O2 content—meaning they do NOT fire in pure anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning where PaO2 remains ~100 mmHg!

open.q: Why do carotid body peripheral chemoreceptors fail to stimulate ventilation in moderate anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning?
accept: Carotid bodies have extremely high blood flow relative to metabolic demand and respond to dissolved arterial PaO2 rather than O2 content; PaO2 remains normal (~100 mmHg) in anemia and CO poisoning
They sense dissolved PaO2 (which stays normal) rather than bound O2 content

questions.q: How does the ventilatory response to declining arterial PaO2 behave when PaCO2 is held constant at 40 mmHg versus when PaCO2 is elevated (hypercapnia)?
options: Ventilation rises sharply when PaO₂ falls below about 60 mmHg; hypercapnia potentiates this hypoxic response
Ventilation rises linearly as PaO₂ falls from 100 mmHg, regardless of PaCO₂
Hypercapnia suppresses carotid body activity and abolishes the hypoxic response
Ventilation falls when PaO₂ drops below 60 mmHg because peripheral chemoreceptors are inhibited
questions.explain: Synergistic interaction between hypoxia and hypercapnia/acidosis at the carotid bodies dramatically amplifies minute ventilation in asphyxia (simultaneous hypoxia + hypercapnia).

open.q: At approximately what arterial PaO2 threshold does the hypoxic ventilatory drive begin to rise steeply during isocapnic hypoxia, and how does concurrent hypercapnia affect this curve?
accept: Below ~60 mmHg; concurrent hypercapnia potentiates/steepens the ventilatory response to hypoxia
~60 mmHg; hypercapnia amplifies the hypoxic ventilatory response

questions.q: Why does chronic hypercapnia (e.g., severe COPD with persistent PaCO2 = 60 mmHg) blunt the central chemoreceptor ventilatory response to CO2 over several days?
options: CSF HCO3− rises, buffering H+ and blunting central CO2 drive
CSF bicarbonate falls progressively, increasing acidity and amplifying the central response to CO₂
Central chemoreceptors become insensitive because high CO₂ destroys medullary neurons
Carotid bodies stop releasing neurotransmitters after several days of elevated PaCO₂
questions.explain: Because central chemoreceptors sense CSF [H+] rather than CO2 directly, renal and choroid-plexus HCO3- compensation resets central CO2 sensitivity to a higher PaCO2 setpoint. Key detail: CSF bicarbonate rises over time, partly correcting pH and reducing central chemoreceptor stimulation despite persistent hypercapnia.

open.q: Explain why central chemoreceptor sensitivity to elevated PaCO2 decreases in patients with chronic respiratory acidosis (such as chronic hypercapnic COPD).
accept: Bicarbonate (HCO3-) accumulates in CSF (via choroid plexus transport and renal HCO3- retention) over 24-72 hours, buffering CSF [H+] back toward normal and removing the central acid stimulus
CSF HCO3- elevation normalizes CSF pH despite persistent hypercapnia

questions.sub: Pulmonary and Airway Reflexes (Hering-Breuer, J-Receptors, Irritant)
questions.q: What is the 'Hering-Breuer inflation reflex', which receptors and afferent fibers mediate it, and when is it physiologically active in humans?
options: Slowly adapting airway stretch receptors signal via the vagus to inhibit inspiration
Rapidly adapting nasal receptors trigger sneezing through the trigeminal nerve
Alveolar J-receptors trigger prolonged breath-holding during inflation
Carotid baroreceptors increase tidal volume when blood pressure rises
questions.explain: Conversely, the Hering-Breuer deflation reflex triggers inspiratory effort when the lung is markedly deflated (as in pneumothorax or atelectasis). Key detail: Slowly adapting airway stretch receptors send vagal afferents that inhibit inspiration during marked lung inflation.

open.q: Describe the stimulus, receptor type, afferent pathway, and reflex effect of the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex.
accept: Marked lung inflation (>1-1.5 L in adults) stimulates slowly adapting airway smooth muscle stretch receptors, sending signals via myelinated vagal (CN X) fibers to inhibit inspiration and prevent overinflation
Lung stretch -> slowly adapting airway stretch receptors -> vagus nerve -> inhibition of inspiration

questions.sub: Pulmonary and Airway Reflexes (Hering-Breuer, J-Receptors, Irritant)
questions.q: Where are 'J-receptors' (juxtapulmonary capillary receptors) located, which nerve fibers transmit their signals, and what clinical conditions stimulate them?
options: Alveolar-capillary J-receptors send vagal C-fibre signals that cause rapid, shallow breathing
Diaphragm tendon; phrenic motor fibres; muscle stretch triggers prolonged inspiratory tetany
Carotid body; glossopharyngeal fibres; increased PaO₂ triggers expiratory apnoea
Tracheal mucosa; hypoglossal fibres; cold air triggers sustained diaphragmatic contraction
questions.explain: Paintal discovered J-receptors; interstitial fluid accumulation in left heart failure or pulmonary embolism stretches alveolar-capillary interstitium and triggers vagal C-fiber tachypnea and air hunger. Key detail: Alveolar walls near pulmonary capillaries; vagal C-fibres; pulmonary congestion or interstitial oedema triggers rapid shallow breathing.

open.q: State the anatomical location, afferent nerve fiber type, physiological stimuli, and respiratory response of pulmonary J-receptors.
accept: Alveolar walls adjacent to pulmonary capillaries; unmyelinated vagal C-fibers; stimulated by pulmonary vascular congestion, interstitial edema, or microemboli; causes rapid shallow breathing (tachypnea) and dyspnea
Alveolar-capillary interstitium; vagal C-fibers; pulmonary edema/congestion -> tachypnea and dyspnea

questions.sub: Pulmonary and Airway Reflexes (Hering-Breuer, J-Receptors, Irritant)
questions.q: What are 'rapidly adapting irritant receptors' in the airway epithelium, and what protective reflexes do they elicit?
options: Vagal irritant afferents trigger cough, bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion and tachypnoea
Unmyelinated sympathetic fibers causing bronchodilation during sleep
Stretch receptors in the stomach causing hiccups
Chemoreceptors in the kidney causing erythropoietin release
questions.explain: In the larynx and trachea, irritant receptor stimulation elicits vigorous coughing and laryngospasm, whereas nasal mucosal irritation (CN V) elicits sneezing with pharyngeal depression to direct airflow through the nose. Key detail: Myelinated vagal afferents between epithelial cells; stimulated by smoke, dust, cold air, noxious gases, or histamine; trigger cough, bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, and tachypnea.

open.q: List three stimuli and three reflex responses mediated by airway rapidly adapting irritant receptors.
accept: Stimuli: inhaled smoke/dust, noxious gases, cold air, histamine; Responses: coughing, bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, tachypnea
Smoke, dust, chemical irritants -> cough, bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion

questions.sub: Pulmonary and Airway Reflexes (Hering-Breuer, J-Receptors, Irritant)
questions.q: What is the 'Head's paradoxical reflex' in newborn infants?
options: Sudden lung inflation in a newborn triggers a brief, deep augmented inspiratory gasp (not inhibition), helping open fluid-filled alveoli and establish FRC at birth
Lung deflation causes immediate apnea for 5 minutes
Cold air causes complete paralysis of the diaphragm
Swallowing triggers simultaneous inspiration
questions.explain: Head's paradoxical reflex (also seen in occasional periodic 'sighs' in adults) recruits collapsed alveoli and spreads pulmonary surfactant across the alveolar surface.

open.q: What is Head's paradoxical reflex, and what is its physiological role in neonates and periodic adult sighs?
accept: A brief, augmented inspiratory gasp triggered by sudden lung inflation; helps expand uninflated alveoli at birth and periodically re-expands atelectatic alveoli (sighs) in adults
Inflation-induced augmented inspiratory effort that recruits collapsed alveoli

questions.sub: Voluntary Control, Corticospinal Pathways, and Behavioral Breathing
questions.q: How can humans voluntarily hold their breath, speak, sing, or hyperventilate despite automatic brainstem respiratory rhythmogenesis?
options: Corticospinal pathways allow voluntary control of respiratory muscles until chemical drive overrides breath-holding
Voluntary breathing is controlled exclusively by the cerebellum and vagus nerve
The cortex permanently suppresses the medullary rhythm generator during speech
Humans cannot voluntarily change breathing rate or depth
questions.explain: Because voluntary corticospinal pathways and automatic medullary bulbospinal pathways are anatomically separate in the spinal cord, selective lesions can abolish one while sparing the other.

open.q: Which descending spinal tract carries voluntary cortical control of breathing, and why is it impossible to hold one's breath until death at sea level?
accept: Corticospinal tract; rising PaCO2 and falling PaO2 stimulate chemoreceptors until they reach the breaking point and involuntarily override cortical breath-holding
Corticospinal tract; rising PaCO2/falling PaO2 reaches the chemoreceptor breaking point

questions.q: At the exact onset (within the first 1-2 seconds) of dynamic exercise, minute ventilation jumps abruptly BEFORE arterial PaO2, PaCO2, or pH have had time to change. Which mechanisms drive this rapid 'Phase I' neural component of exercise hyperpnea?
options: Central command and limb/joint proprioceptor input raise ventilation immediately at exercise onset
Severe arterial hypoxemia (PaO2 = 30 mmHg) within 0.5 seconds of starting to walk
Marked arterial hypercapnia (PaCO2 = 75 mmHg) during the first step
Sudden drop in arterial pH to 7.05
questions.explain: In moderate steady-state exercise, mean arterial PaO2, PaCO2, and pH remain virtually identical to resting values—proving that central command, limb mechanoreceptors/metaboreceptors, and fine-tuned breath-by-breath oscillation sensing match ventilation to metabolic rate. Key detail: Feedforward central command from motor cortex/hypothalamus to brainstem respiratory centers plus proprioceptive mechanoreceptor feedback from moving limbs and joints.

open.q: Name the two primary neural mechanisms responsible for the immediate abrupt rise in ventilation at the onset of exercise before blood gases change.
accept: Central command (feedforward motor cortex signals to brainstem respiratory centers) and proprioceptive feedback from exercising limbs/joints
Central command and limb/joint proprioceptor afferents

questions.sub: Pulmonary and Airway Reflexes (Hering-Breuer, J-Receptors, Irritant)
questions.q: What are the sequential mechanical phases of a normal physiological cough reflex?
options: Deep inspiration → glottic closure → pressure-building expiration → sudden glottic opening and rapid airflow
Deep inspiration → glottic opening → passive expiration → closure of the vocal folds
Glottic closure → quiet expiration → diaphragmatic relaxation → swallowing
Passive expiration → glottic closure → bronchial dilation → slow nasal inspiration
questions.explain: High intrathoracic pressure compresses the posterior non-cartilaginous trachealis membrane inward, narrowing airway cross-section to maximize linear airflow velocity and shear force.

open.q: Outline the four sequential mechanical steps of an effective cough reflex.
accept: 1) Deep inspiration; 2) Closure of the glottis; 3) Forceful contraction of expiratory muscles building high intrathoracic pressure; 4) Sudden glottic opening producing high-velocity expulsive airflow
Deep inspiration -> glottic closure -> expiratory muscle contraction/high intrathoracic pressure -> sudden glottic opening

questions.q: What is 'Kussmaul respiration', what metabolic disturbance classically triggers it, and which chemoreceptors mediate it?
options: Deep, rapid breathing in severe metabolic acidosis, driven mainly by carotid bodies
Alternating cycles of crescendo-decrescendo breathing and apnea caused by heart failure
Prolonged inspiratory spasms caused by mid-pontine stroke
Completely irregular ataxic breathing caused by medullary compression
questions.explain: Because arterial H+ crosses the blood-brain barrier slowly, peripheral carotid body chemoreceptors initiate rapid Kussmaul hyperventilation to lower PaCO2 and compensate for metabolic acidemia. Key detail: Deep, rapid hyperventilation ('air hunger') driven by severe metabolic acidosis (diabetic ketoacidosis, uremia, lactic acidosis) via peripheral carotid body chemoreceptors sensing elevated arterial [H+].

open.q: Describe Kussmaul breathing, name its classic metabolic trigger, and identify the primary chemoreceptor group that initiates it.
accept: Deep, rapid hyperventilation triggered by severe metabolic acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis), mediated primarily by peripheral carotid body chemoreceptors responding to high arterial [H+]
Deep rapid breathing in severe metabolic acidosis; peripheral carotid body chemoreceptors

questions.q: How do 'Cheyne-Stokes respiration' and 'Biot's (ataxic) respiration' differ in rhythm and neuroanatomical/pathophysiological cause?
options: Cheyne–Stokes: cyclic waxing/waning with regular apnoea (CHF/forebrain/altitude); Biot's: erratic breaths and random pauses (medullary lesion)
Cheyne–Stokes: erratic breaths and random pauses (medullary lesion); Biot's: waxing/waning with regular apnoea (CHF/forebrain)
Cheyne–Stokes: deep rapid breathing in metabolic acidosis; Biot's: prolonged inspiratory pauses after pontine injury
Cheyne–Stokes: prolonged inspiratory spasms from pontine injury; Biot's: periodic crescendo–decrescendo breathing in heart failure
questions.explain: Biot's (ataxic) breathing signals life-threatening medullary brainstem compression/ischemia (e.g., cerebellar hemorrhage or uncal/tonsillar herniation) and often heralds imminent respiratory arrest. Key detail: Cheyne-Stokes: rhythmic crescendo-decrescendo tidal volumes with regular apneas (heart failure, forebrain injury, altitude); Biot's: completely irregular gasps and random pauses from direct medullary damage.

open.q: Contrast the breathing pattern and anatomical/clinical causes of Cheyne-Stokes respiration versus Biot's (ataxic) respiration.
accept: Cheyne-Stokes: rhythmic crescendo-decrescendo tidal volumes alternating with regular apneas (heart failure with delayed circulation time, bilateral forebrain injury, high altitude); Biot's: completely irregular, erratic breaths and random apneas (direct medullary damage)
Cyclic waxing-waning with regular apnea (heart failure/forebrain/altitude) vs erratic unpredictable breaths/pauses (medullary lesion)

questions.q: Why does severe congestive heart failure (CHF) predispose patients to Cheyne-Stokes respiration?
options: Low cardiac output delays blood-gas feedback, causing cyclic ventilatory overshoot and undershoot
Heart failure increases carotid body blood flow tenfold
Heart failure paralyzes the phrenic nerve on the left side
Heart failure lowers arterial PCO2 to 5 mmHg permanently
questions.explain: In engineering control theory, adding a long transport delay (low cardiac output) to a high-gain feedback loop destabilizes steady-state ventilation into oscillatory crescendo-decrescendo cycles. Key detail: Prolonged lung-to-chemoreceptor circulation time phase-lags the negative-feedback loop, causing cyclic ventilatory overshoot and undershoot.

open.q: Explain how low cardiac output in severe heart failure generates Cheyne-Stokes periodic breathing.
accept: Slow circulation time delays transit of blood gas changes from the lungs to the chemoreceptors, creating a phase lag that causes repetitive ventilatory overshoot and apnea undershoot
Prolonged lung-to-chemoreceptor circulation delay destabilizes negative-feedback respiratory control

questions.sub: Pulmonary and Airway Reflexes (Hering-Breuer, J-Receptors, Irritant)
questions.q: How is respiration coordinated with swallowing (deglutition) to prevent pulmonary aspiration?
options: Medullary swallowing circuits briefly inhibit breathing and close the glottis
Swallowing triggers maximal deep inspiration
The vocal cords open widely during the pharyngeal swallow
Respiration and swallowing are completely uncoordinated in healthy adults
questions.explain: Brief deglutition apnea (typically occurring during expiration so post-swallow exhalation clears any pharyngeal residue) protects the lower airway from food or liquid aspiration. Key detail: Medullary swallowing centers reflexively inhibit respiration (deglutition apnea ~0.5-1.5 s), elevate the larynx, close the vocal cords, and fold the epiglottis over the laryngeal inlet.

open.q: What is 'deglutition apnea', and how does it protect the respiratory tract during swallowing?
accept: Temporary reflex inhibition of breathing during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing (accompanied by glottic closure and epiglottic retroflexion) that prevents aspiration into the trachea
Brief reflex cessation of respiration with glottic closure during swallowing to prevent aspiration

questions.q: How do body temperature (fever) and hormones such as progesterone influence alveolar ventilation?
options: Fever and progesterone stimulate ventilation; pregnancy lowers resting PaCO2 to about 30 mmHg
Progesterone depresses respiration and raises PaCO2 to 65 mmHg during pregnancy
Fever slows respiratory rate to 4 breaths/min
Neither temperature nor hormones affect brainstem respiratory neurons
questions.explain: Progesterone directly increases central chemoreceptor sensitivity to CO2, driving mild gestational hyperventilation (PaCO2 ~30 mmHg) that creates a favorable CO2 diffusion gradient from fetus to mother. Key detail: Fever (via hypothalamic projections) and progesterone (luteal phase/pregnancy) both stimulate ventilation and lower resting PaCO2 (to ~30-32 mmHg in pregnancy).

open.q: How does progesterone affect central chemoreceptor sensitivity and resting arterial PaCO2 during pregnancy?
accept: Progesterone increases respiratory center sensitivity to CO2, stimulating hyperventilation and lowering resting maternal PaCO2 to ~30 mmHg
Increases CO2 sensitivity and ventilation, lowering PaCO2 to ~30 mmHg

questions.q: What happens to the dorsal and ventral medullary respiratory centers and ventilation when high-dose opioids (e.g., morphine, fentanyl) or barbiturates are administered?
options: Mu-opioid inhibition of medullary/pre-Bötzinger neurons depresses respiratory rhythm and chemoreflexes
Opioids strongly stimulate the pre-Botzinger complex to cause hyperventilation
Opioids selectively paralyze only the diaphragm while sparing the pons
Opioids increase sensitivity to CO2 by 300%
questions.explain: Opioid-induced respiratory depression slows respiratory rate first (bradypnea) and abolishes hypoxic/hypercapnic arousal, reversed competitively by the mu-receptor antagonist naloxone. Key detail: Opioids activate mu-opioid receptors on pre-Botzinger and medullary/pontine neurons, depressing rhythmogenesis, blunting hypercapnic and hypoxic chemoreflexes, and reducing rate and tidal volume.

open.q: Explain the neurochemical mechanism by which opioids cause respiratory depression and shift the CO2 ventilatory response curve.
accept: Activation of mu-opioid receptors inhibits pre-Botzinger pacemaker and brainstem respiratory neurons, depressing rhythm generation and shifting the CO2 ventilatory response curve downward and to the right
Mu-opioid receptor inhibition of brainstem respiratory neurons, reducing rate and blunting hypercapnic/hypoxic drive

questions.sub: Voluntary Control, Corticospinal Pathways, and Behavioral Breathing
questions.q: How do the 'limbic system' and 'pain/emotional afferents' modulate breathing?
options: Limbic and hypothalamic inputs can alter breathing during emotion or pain, sometimes causing hyperventilation
Emotional stress permanently stops diaphragmatic movement
Limbic projections act only on renal tubules
Pain always causes hypoventilation with extreme hypercapnia
questions.explain: Panic-induced hyperventilation blows off CO2, causing cerebral vasoconstriction (lightheadedness) and increased albumin binding of Ca2+ (perioral tingling and carpopedal tetany).

open.q: Explain why acute anxiety-induced hyperventilation causes lightheadedness and perioral/digital paresthesias.
accept: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 (hypocapnia), causing cerebral vasoconstriction (lightheadedness) and respiratory alkalosis that increases Ca2+ binding to albumin (lowering ionized Ca2+ and causing neuronal hyperexcitability/paresthesias)
Hypocapnic cerebral vasoconstriction and alkalosis-induced decrease in free ionized calcium

questions.q: What is the 'dorsal-ventral respiratory group rhythm-switching' role of Botzinger complex expiratory neurons?
options: Botzinger expiratory neurons inhibit inspiratory neurons, enforcing phase alternation
They innervate the gastrocnemius muscle during running
They secrete surfactant into the alveoli
They stimulate aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex
questions.explain: Reciprocal inhibition between inspiratory pre-Botzinger/rVRG neurons and expiratory Botzinger neurons prevents simultaneous co-contraction of inspiratory and expiratory muscles. Key detail: Glycinergic/GABAergic expiratory neurons inhibit inspiratory pre-Botzinger and DRG neurons during expiration, enforcing reciprocal alternation.

open.q: What is the role of the medullary Botzinger complex in the respiratory cycle?
accept: Contains inhibitory expiratory neurons that suppress inspiratory neurons during expiration to enforce reciprocal phase alternation

questions.q: A 19-year-old man with a congenital PHOX2B gene mutation has normal breathing while awake (able to speak, exercise, and voluntarily breathe normally), but develops severe hypoventilation, hypercapnia (PaCO2 78 mmHg), and life-threatening apnea whenever he falls asleep ('Ondine's curse' / congenital central hypoventilation syndrome). What neuroanatomical dissociation explains his presentation?
options: Automatic brainstem respiratory drive fails during sleep; voluntary cortical breathing remains intact when awake
Bilateral phrenic nerve transection
Complete destruction of the primary motor cortex
Severe emphysema with bullous air trapping
questions.explain: Ondine's curse (congenital or acquired brainstem lesion damaging automatic medullary chemoreception/rhythmogenesis) demonstrates the anatomical independence of voluntary cortical versus automatic metabolic respiratory pathways. Key detail: Selective failure of automatic brainstem chemoreceptor/rhythm control (retrotrapezoid nucleus/pre-Botzinger) with intact voluntary corticospinal breathing during wakefulness.

open.q: What is Ondine's curse (central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome), and which respiratory control system fails while another remains intact?
accept: Loss of automatic/metabolic brainstem respiratory drive (causing severe hypoventilation/apnea during sleep) with preservation of voluntary cortical control during wakefulness
Failure of automatic brainstem chemoreceptor/rhythm drive during sleep while voluntary corticospinal breathing remains intact awake

questions.q: A 61-year-old man sustains a pontine hemorrhage in the mid-to-lower pons. On neurological examination, he exhibits sustained, deep inspiratory pauses lasting 10-15 seconds followed by brief expiratory gasps (apneustic breathing). Which brainstem structure was damaged?
options: The upper pontine pneumotaxic center (parabrachial / Kolliker-Fuse region), leaving the lower pontine apneustic center uninhibited
The pre-Botzinger complex in the caudal medulla
The left phrenic nerve root at C4
The carotid sinus baroreceptors
questions.explain: Lesions disconnecting the rostral pontine pneumotaxic center release prolonged inspiratory drive from the caudal pontine apneustic center.

open.q: Which brainstem center is damaged when a pontine stroke produces apneustic breathing (prolonged inspiratory pauses)?
accept: The pneumotaxic center in the upper (rostral) pons

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with vomiting, fruity breath, arterial pH 7.14, PaCO2 18 mmHg, HCO3- 6 mEq/L, and deep, rapid respirations at 32 breaths/min (Kussmaul breathing). Which receptors initiated her compensatory hyperventilation, and what would happen if she were heavily sedated or given a paralytic without mechanical ventilation?
options: Carotid bodies sense arterial acidaemia; suppressing compensation worsens diabetic ketoacidosis
Central chemoreceptors respond directly to high arterial bicarbonate
Pulmonary J-receptors detect alkalosis and initiate Kussmaul breathing
High arterial oxygen is the primary stimulus for Kussmaul breathing
questions.explain: In severe metabolic acidosis, peripheral carotid body hyperventilation is a vital life-saving compensation; allowing PaCO2 to normalize removes respiratory compensation and causes lethal blood pH collapse. Key detail: Peripheral chemoreceptors detect arterial acidaemia and stimulate hyperventilation; suppressing it can cause dangerous worsening of acidemia.

open.q: Why are peripheral carotid body chemoreceptors—rather than central chemoreceptors—the primary drivers of Kussmaul hyperventilation in acute diabetic ketoacidosis?
accept: Fixed metabolic acids (ketoacids / H+) cross the blood-brain barrier very slowly, whereas peripheral carotid bodies are directly exposed to arterial blood and respond immediately to falling arterial pH
H+ ions cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, so peripheral carotid bodies sense arterial acidemia directly

questions.q: A 68-year-old man with severe ischemic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction 18%) is observed by his wife during sleep to have recurring 50-second cycles in which his breathing gradually waxes deeper and faster, then wanes and stops completely for 15 seconds before starting again. Polysomnography shows absence of respiratory effort during the apneas. What is this pattern and its underlying mechanism?
options: Cheyne–Stokes central apnoea: waxing/waning breathing with absent effort during pauses
Obstructive sleep apnea caused by tonsillar hypertrophy
Biot's ataxic breathing from cerebellar herniation
Apneustic breathing from mid-pontine infarction
questions.explain: Unlike obstructive sleep apnea (where chest/abdominal efforts continue against a collapsed pharynx), Cheyne-Stokes respiration in heart failure is a central apnea driven by circulatory delay between pulmonary gas exchange and chemoreceptors. Key detail: Cheyne-Stokes central sleep apnea from prolonged lung-to-brain circulatory delay and heightened chemoreceptor loop gain in severe systolic heart failure.

open.q: How does Cheyne-Stokes central sleep apnea in heart failure differ from obstructive sleep apnea in terms of respiratory muscle effort during the apneic pause?
accept: In Cheyne-Stokes central apnea, brainstem respiratory drive and thoracoabdominal muscle effort cease completely during the pause; in obstructive sleep apnea, thoracoabdominal respiratory effort continues against an occluded upper airway
Absent respiratory effort (central Cheyne-Stokes) vs continued effort against a blocked airway (obstructive)

questions.q: A 52-year-old man undergoes bilateral carotid body tumor (paraganglioma) resection. Postoperatively, his resting PaCO2 is 42 mmHg on room air, but when exposed to mild hypoxia (breathing 12% O2), he fails to increase his minute ventilation and develops progressive severe hypoxemia. Why is his hypoxic ventilatory drive completely absent while his hypercapnic drive remains ~70-80% intact?
options: Carotid bodies mediate hypoxic drive; central medullary chemoreceptors preserve most CO2 drive
Central medullary chemoreceptors detect hypoxia exclusively
Aortic bodies control 100% of CO2 sensitivity
Bilateral carotid body resection transects the phrenic nerves
questions.explain: Bilateral carotid body denervation abolishes the hypoxic ventilatory drive in humans while preserving the majority of the hypercapnic drive via intact central medullary chemoreceptors. Key detail: Carotid bodies are the sole chemoreceptors mediating the hypoxic ventilatory response, whereas intact central medullary chemoreceptors account for ~70-80% of the CO2 ventilatory response.

open.q: What happens to the ventilatory responses to hypoxia versus hypercapnia in a patient after bilateral carotid body resection?
accept: The hypoxic ventilatory response is completely abolished, while the hypercapnic (CO2) ventilatory response remains largely preserved (~70-80%) via intact central medullary chemoreceptors
Hypoxic drive is lost; hypercapnic drive is mostly preserved

questions.q: In which nucleus of the medulla is the dorsal respiratory group located?
options: Nucleus tractus solitarius
Nucleus ambiguus
Inferior olivary nucleus
Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus
questions.explain: The dorsal respiratory group lies in the nucleus tractus solitarius, receives vagal and glossopharyngeal afferents, and mainly drives inspiration.

open.q: In which medullary nucleus is the dorsal respiratory group located?

questions.q: Which medullary group of neurons is largely inactive in quiet breathing and is recruited for forced expiration and forced inspiration?
options: Dorsal respiratory group
Ventral respiratory group
Apneustic centre
Pneumotaxic centre
questions.explain: The ventral respiratory group contains both inspiratory and expiratory neurons that become active when ventilation needs to rise. The dorsal group is the main driver of quiet inspiration.

open.q: Which medullary group of neurons is largely inactive in quiet breathing and is recruited for forced expiration and forced inspiration?

questions.q: The pre-Botzinger complex in the rostral ventral medulla is thought to act as the:
options: Sensor of arterial oxygen
Relay for lung stretch signals
Centre for the cough reflex
Respiratory rhythm generator
questions.explain: The pre-Botzinger complex contains pacemaker-like neurons that generate the basic rhythm of breathing. Other brainstem areas modify that rhythm.

open.q: What is the proposed role of the pre-Botzinger complex in the ventral medulla?

questions.q: In which part of the brainstem is the pneumotaxic centre located?
options: Upper pons
Lower pons
Medulla oblongata
Midbrain
questions.explain: The pneumotaxic centre lies in the nucleus parabrachialis medialis and Kolliker-Fuse nucleus of the upper pons. The apneustic centre is in the lower pons.

open.q: In which part of the brainstem is the pneumotaxic centre located?

questions.q: What is the main effect of the pneumotaxic centre on inspiration?
options: Prolongs inspiratory gasps
Detects arterial hypoxia
Shortens each inspiration
Drives forced expiration
questions.explain: The pneumotaxic centre switches off the inspiratory ramp early, which limits tidal volume and raises the respiratory rate. Prolonged inspiratory gasps are the feature of the apneustic centre.

open.q: What is the main effect of the pneumotaxic centre on inspiration?

questions.q: Which breathing pattern, with prolonged inspiratory gasps and brief expiration, follows mid-pontine transection together with bilateral vagotomy?
options: Cheyne-Stokes breathing
Apneusis
Kussmaul breathing
Complete apnoea
questions.explain: Removing both pneumotaxic input and vagal inhibition leaves the apneustic centre unopposed. Inspiration is then held for long periods.

open.q: What is the name of the breathing pattern of prolonged inspiratory gasps with brief expiration seen after mid-pontine transection with bilateral vagotomy?

questions.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors located?
options: Bifurcation of the common carotid
Arch of the aorta
Ventral surface of the medulla
Wall of the left atrium
questions.explain: Central chemoreceptors lie in a chemosensitive area on the ventral medullary surface, bathed by cerebrospinal fluid. The carotid and aortic bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors.

open.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors located?

questions.q: What directly stimulates the central chemoreceptors?
options: Hydrogen ions in the CSF
Low arterial oxygen tension
Low arterial blood pressure
High plasma sodium
questions.explain: CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier, forms carbonic acid in the CSF and releases H+, which excites the chemoreceptors. Low arterial PO2 acts on the peripheral chemoreceptors instead.

open.q: What directly stimulates the central chemoreceptors?
accept: Hydrogen ion concentration in brain extracellular fluid

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries afferent fibres from the carotid body to the medulla?
options: Cranial nerve X
Cranial nerve XII
Cranial nerve IX
Cranial nerve V
questions.explain: Carotid body afferents run in the carotid sinus nerve of Hering, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

open.q: Which cranial nerve carries afferent fibres from the carotid body to the medulla?

questions.q: Aortic body chemoreceptors send their afferent signals to the medulla through which nerve?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
Phrenic nerve
Trigeminal nerve
Vagus nerve
questions.explain: Aortic body afferents travel in the vagus nerve (CN X). Students often confuse this with the carotid body, which uses the glossopharyngeal nerve.

open.q: Aortic body chemoreceptors send their afferent signals to the medulla through which nerve?

questions.q: Which cells in the carotid body detect a fall in arterial PO2?
options: Sustentacular cells
Type I glomus cells
Type II pneumocytes
Kupffer cells
questions.explain: Type I glomus cells sense hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis and release neurotransmitter onto afferent nerve endings. Type II (sustentacular) cells are supporting cells.

open.q: Which cells in the carotid body detect a fall in arterial PO2?
accept: Chemoreceptor cells of the carotid body

questions.q: Peripheral chemoreceptors cause a marked rise in ventilation when arterial PO2 falls below approximately:
options: 100 mmHg
80 mmHg
60 mmHg
20 mmHg
questions.explain: Ventilation changes little until PaO2 falls below about 60 mmHg (8 kPa), after which it rises steeply.

open.q: Under approximately what arterial PO2 do the peripheral chemoreceptors cause a marked rise in ventilation?

questions.q: Under normal conditions, which blood gas variable is the most important regulator of minute ventilation?
options: Arterial PO2
Arterial PCO2
Plasma bicarbonate
Haemoglobin concentration
questions.explain: Ventilation rises almost linearly with PaCO2, mostly through the central chemoreceptors. PaO2 only matters once it falls below about 60 mmHg.

open.q: Under normal conditions, which blood gas variable is the most important regulator of minute ventilation?

questions.q: A patient with carbon monoxide poisoning has severe tissue hypoxia but is not hyperventilating. Why?
options: Arterial PO2 is still normal
CO paralyses the carotid nerves
Central chemoreceptors are inhibited
Carbon monoxide raises arterial pH
questions.explain: Carotid bodies respond to the dissolved oxygen tension, not to oxygen content. Their blood flow is very high, so in CO poisoning and anaemia PaO2 stays normal and they are not stimulated.

open.q: A patient with carbon monoxide poisoning has severe tissue hypoxia but is not hyperventilating. Why?
accept: Chemoreceptors sense PO2 not oxygen content

questions.q: The stretch receptors of the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex lie in the:
options: Alveolar wall capillaries
Carotid sinus wall
Diaphragmatic tendons
Airway smooth muscle
questions.explain: Slowly adapting stretch receptors in the smooth muscle of the bronchi and bronchioles send signals along the vagus nerve to the medulla.

open.q: Where are the stretch receptors of the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex located?
accept: Smooth muscle of bronchi and bronchioles
Walls of the bronchi and bronchioles

questions.q: What is the effect of the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex?
options: Triggers inspiration once the lungs are empty
Dilates the airways during every inspiration
Stops inspiration at a high lung volume
Raises heart rate throughout expiration
questions.explain: When the lungs are stretched, vagal signals switch off the inspiratory ramp. This protects the lungs from overinflation and is most active at large tidal volumes.

open.q: What is the effect of the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex on inspiration?
accept: Terminates inspiration when lungs are stretched
Ends inspiration at high lung volume

questions.q: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are stimulated mainly by:
options: Pulmonary congestion
Arterial hypoxaemia
Low arterial PCO2
High body temperature
questions.explain: J receptors lie in the alveolar walls near the capillaries and fire when interstitial fluid accumulates. This causes rapid shallow breathing and the sensation of dyspnoea.

open.q: What stimulates the juxtacapillary (J) receptors in the lung?

questions.q: Stimulation of airway irritant receptors by smoke or dust causes:
options: Slow deep breathing
Cough and bronchospasm
Reduced airway resistance
Lowered blood pressure
questions.explain: Irritant receptors in the airway epithelium trigger cough, sneezing and bronchoconstriction through vagal reflexes to protect the lungs.

open.q: What reflex responses follow stimulation of airway irritant receptors by smoke or dust?

questions.q: A patient with severe COPD and chronic hypercapnia becomes drowsy with a slow respiratory rate after high-concentration oxygen. Which mechanism is mainly responsible?
options: Fatigue of the diaphragm alone
Stimulation of the J receptors
Activation of the Hering-Breuer reflex
Loss of hypoxic ventilatory drive
questions.explain: In chronic CO2 retainers the central chemoreceptors are blunted, so hypoxia becomes the main drive. High-flow oxygen removes it and ventilation falls, so oxygen should be titrated.

open.q: A patient with severe COPD and chronic hypercapnia becomes drowsy with a slow respiratory rate after high-concentration oxygen. Which mechanism is mainly responsible?
accept: Loss of peripheral chemoreceptor hypoxic stimulus

questions.q: A climber ascends rapidly to 4500 m and hyperventilates. Which acid-base disturbance develops first?
options: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.explain: Hypoxia stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors, so PaCO2 falls and pH rises. The alkalosis restrains ventilation until the kidneys excrete bicarbonate over the next days.

open.q: A climber ascends rapidly to 4500 m and hyperventilates. Which acid-base disturbance develops first?

questions.q: After several days of chronic hypercapnia, central chemoreceptor sensitivity to CO2 is blunted. What is the main reason?
options: CSF bicarbonate rises and buffers H+
Peripheral chemoreceptors degenerate
CO2 stops crossing the blood-brain barrier
Vagal afferents are lost
questions.explain: The choroid plexus and brain raise CSF bicarbonate, so CSF pH returns toward normal despite the high PCO2. The H+ stimulus to the chemoreceptors is therefore reduced.

open.q: After several days of chronic hypercapnia, central chemoreceptor sensitivity to CO2 is blunted. What is the main reason?

questions.q: Why does a rise in arterial PCO2 stimulate central chemoreceptors more than an equal rise in plasma H+?
options: H+ passes the blood-brain barrier readily
CO2 diffuses readily into the CSF
CO2 acts only on the carotid body cells
Plasma bicarbonate enters CSF and releases H+
questions.explain: CO2 is lipid soluble and crosses the blood-brain barrier easily, then forms H+ in the CSF. H+ and bicarbonate in plasma cross it very poorly.

open.q: Why does a rise in arterial PCO2 stimulate central chemoreceptors more than an equal rise in plasma H+?
accept: CO2 diffuses into CSF forming H+
H+ cannot cross the blood-brain barrier

questions.q: A patient with severe heart failure has cycles of waxing and waning breathing with apnoeic pauses between them. What is this pattern called?
options: Kussmaul breathing
Biot's breathing
Apneustic breathing
Cheyne-Stokes
questions.explain: Delayed circulation time and raised chemoreceptor gain make PaCO2 overshoot and undershoot, so breathing cycles up and down. Kussmaul breathing is deep and sighing, as in metabolic acidosis.

open.q: A patient with severe heart failure has cycles of waxing and waning breathing with apnoeic pauses between them. What is this pattern called?

questions.q: A patient with a heroin overdose has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6 per minute. Which structures are most directly depressed?
options: Medullary respiratory neurons
Carotid body only
Bronchial stretch receptors
Phrenic nerve motor end plates
questions.explain: Opioids act on mu receptors in the medullary respiratory neurons, including the pre-Botzinger complex, and blunt the response to CO2. Naloxone reverses this.

open.q: A patient with a heroin overdose has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6 per minute. Which brainstem structures are most directly depressed?

questions.q: During moderate exercise, arterial PO2, PCO2 and pH in a healthy person:
options: PCO2 rises steeply
pH rises markedly
Stay close to resting values
PO2 falls below 60 mmHg
questions.explain: Neurogenic drive from the motor cortex and signals from muscle and joint proprioceptors match ventilation to metabolic rate. Blood gases change little until heavy exercise causes lactic acidosis.

open.q: How do arterial PO2, PCO2 and pH change in a healthy person during moderate exercise?

questions.q: Voluntary control of breathing, such as deliberate breath-holding, originates in the:
options: Cerebellar vermis
Thalamic nuclei
Hypothalamic nuclei
Cerebral cortex
questions.explain: Corticospinal fibres from the cerebral cortex act on respiratory motor neurons directly and can override the automatic medullary control for a limited time.

open.q: Which part of the brain is responsible for voluntary control of breathing, such as deliberate breath-holding?

questions.q: What ultimately forces a person to resume breathing after a voluntary breath-hold?
options: Falling blood pressure at the carotid sinus
Rising PaCO2 driving chemoreceptors
Fatigue of the cortical motor neurons
Rising pH stimulating the J receptors
questions.explain: PaCO2 rises (and PaO2 falls) until chemoreceptor drive overcomes voluntary inhibition. This is the breaking point of breath-holding.

open.q: What ultimately forces a person to resume breathing after a voluntary breath-hold?

questions.q: Which spinal cord segments give rise to the phrenic nerve?
questions.explain: The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4 and C5 and supplies the diaphragm. The saying is that C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.

open.q: Which spinal cord segments give rise to the phrenic nerve?

questions.q: A swimmer hyperventilates deeply before an underwater breath-hold. Why does this make blackout more likely?
options: Hyperactive stretch receptors stop breathing
Low PaCO2 delays the urge to breathe
Acidosis abolishes the hypoxic drive
Raised PaO2 permanently damages chemoreceptors
questions.explain: Hyperventilation washes out CO2 but adds little oxygen. The CO2 stimulus to breathe is delayed, so PaO2 can fall to dangerous levels before the swimmer feels the urge to surface.

open.q: A swimmer hyperventilates deeply before an underwater breath-hold. Why does this make blackout more likely?
accept: Lowered PaCO2 delays the urge to breathe
Hypocapnia suppresses the drive to breathe
Hypoxia develops before the CO2 stimulus

questions.q: Bilateral vagotomy with the pons intact produces breathing that is:
options: Rapid and shallow
Irregular with apnoea
Absent altogether
Slow and deep
questions.explain: Without vagal Hering-Breuer feedback, inspiration lasts longer before the pneumotaxic centre ends it. Breathing therefore becomes slower and deeper.

open.q: What change in breathing follows bilateral vagotomy with the pons intact?
